questions.question: Why is the original quote inaccurate?

The lift rental was billed to the wrong account
It was based on an outdated site layout

questions.explanation: Mr. Tsai explains that forty hours came from the old warehouse layout, while Harkness moved to a three-floor site in March. The hourly rate is never questioned, only the number of hours estimated.

questions.question: At 15:49, what does Ms. Vega most likely mean when she writes, "That conversation is on sales, not engineering"?

Engineering will refuse to revise the document

passage:
NOTICE TO ALL STAFF - Airport Shuttle Schedule Change, Effective 1 October

The company shuttle between the Eastside campus and Halvern International Airport will move to a fixed hourly departure. Under the current system, riders book a seat and the van leaves only when it is full, which has produced waits of up to fifty minutes during afternoon peaks.

From 1 October, the van departs from the north lobby at the top of every hour between 05:00 and 21:00, full or not. Travel time to Terminal 2 averages thirty-five minutes. Add fifteen minutes for Terminal 1.

Booking is still required, but only to guarantee a seat. Log in to the travel portal at least two hours before departure. Walk-up riders may board if seats remain at the moment the van leaves.

Luggage is limited to one checked bag and one carry-on per rider. Riders travelling with equipment cases must arrange a cargo van through the facilities desk at least one business day in advance.

Send questions to shuttle@eastsidecampus.example rather than to the drivers.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the notice?
options: To introduce a newly opened airport terminal
To announce that the shuttle will be discontinued
To ask employees to volunteer as drivers
To explain a change in departure times
questions.explanation: The heading and the first two paragraphs describe the shift from full-van departures to fixed hourly ones. The service is expanding its schedule rather than ending, so the second option is contradicted.

questions.question: What must riders do in order to guarantee a seat?
options: Arrive at the north lobby thirty minutes early
Book through the travel portal two hours ahead
Notify one of the drivers by email
Pay a fee at the facilities desk
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph states that booking remains necessary to guarantee a seat and sets a two-hour portal deadline. The notice also asks staff not to send questions to drivers, so emailing them is wrong.

questions.question: What is implied about the current booking system?
options: It is used mainly by outside visitors
It charges riders a fee for each trip
It has caused long waits for some riders
It will remain in place until December
questions.explanation: Waits of up to fifty minutes during afternoon peaks are given as the reason for replacing the current system. The change takes effect on 1 October, which rules out the option about December.

Hartwell Research Library - Group Study Room Rules

Rooms 2 through 7 are available to any cardholder. Please read the following before your session.

Reserve online. Same-day reservations open at 07:00 and close fifteen minutes before the start of each slot. Slots run two hours. A group may hold one slot per day, and a second slot may be added at the service desk only after 16:00, when demand falls.

Rooms are held for ten minutes. If nobody from your group has arrived by then, staff will release the room to the waiting list posted at the front desk.

Food is not permitted. Lidded drinks are fine. Whiteboards are cleaned nightly, so please do not leave notes you still need. Staff cannot photograph them for you.

Rooms 6 and 7 have video conferencing equipment. Use headphones for any call. Sound carries into the reading room through the upper vents, and this is the single most common complaint we receive.

Report faults to the second-floor desk rather than moving furniture between rooms.

questions.question: When may a group reserve a second study slot?
options: After 16:00, in person at the service desk
At 07:00 on the day of the session
On weekends only
Ten minutes before the first slot ends
questions.explanation: The third paragraph permits a second slot at the service desk only after 16:00, when demand drops. The 07:00 time refers to when same-day online reservations open, not to extra slots.

questions.question: What happens if a group arrives late for a reservation?
options: The group is charged a late fee
The reservation is moved to the following day
The room is given to someone on the waiting list
Staff telephone the cardholder who booked it
questions.explanation: Rooms are held for only ten minutes before staff release them to the posted waiting list. No fee of any kind is mentioned in the notice, so the first option is invented.

questions.question: What does the notice suggest about rooms 6 and 7?
options: They are reserved for library staff members
Noise from them disturbs other library users
They are larger than the other study rooms
They must be booked one week in advance
questions.explanation: Headphones are required because sound from those rooms carries into the reading room and generates the most complaints. Room size is never discussed, so the third option has no basis.

passage:
Warehouses Are Getting Quieter, and That Is the Point

Walk into a regional distribution centre built in the last three years and the first thing you notice is what you do not hear: no shouted aisle numbers, no forklift horns every forty seconds. Goods-to-person systems now bring shelving units to a fixed picking station, so the worker stays in place while the inventory moves.

Operators report picking rates roughly three times higher than in manual aisles, but the more interesting number is turnover. At one grocery distributor in the midlands, annual staff turnover at the picking stations fell from 61 percent to 24 percent after the retrofit. Managers attribute the drop to the walking. A manual picker covered about sixteen kilometres per shift. The same worker now walks under two.

The equipment is not cheap. A mid-size retrofit runs between four and seven million dollars, and most operators need four to six years to recover it. Smaller firms are instead renting robot fleets by the month, an arrangement that barely existed before 2023.

questions.question: What is the article mainly about?
options: A shortage of trained forklift operators
How automation is changing warehouse work
A grocery distributor opening in the midlands
The rising cost of industrial property
questions.explanation: The article moves from quieter facilities to picking rates, turnover, and equipment costs, all consequences of goods-to-person automation. The grocery distributor appears only as a single example, not as the subject.

questions.question: According to the article, what do managers credit for the lower turnover?
options: Higher hourly wages at the picking stations
Shorter shifts for warehouse staff
An improved training program
A large reduction in walking during a shift
questions.explanation: Managers attribute the fall from 61 percent to 24 percent to walking distance dropping from sixteen kilometres per shift to under two. Wages and shift length are never mentioned as factors.

questions.question: What is suggested about smaller firms?
options: They avoid large upfront costs by renting equipment
They recover their investment faster than large operators
They have stopped using goods-to-person systems
They report the highest picking rates in the industry
questions.explanation: Rather than paying four to seven million dollars for a retrofit, smaller firms rent robot fleets monthly. That is the opposite of abandoning the technology, so the third option misreads the final paragraph.

passage:
The Spreadsheet Years Are Ending for Smaller Firms

For two decades, the typical thirty-person manufacturer ran on a shared spreadsheet, a filing cabinet, and one person who knew where everything was. That arrangement is breaking down, and not because the software finally got better.

Three pressures are doing the work. Large customers now require electronic order confirmations, which a spreadsheet cannot produce. Insurers ask for traceability records that take days to assemble by hand. And the person who knew where everything was is retiring.

What firms are buying is smaller than it was a decade ago. Rather than one system covering every department, most start with a single process, usually quoting or inventory, and connect it to whatever else they run. A survey of 400 small manufacturers put the median first-year spend at 31,000 dollars, well below the six-figure projects that dominated earlier coverage.

The failures share a pattern. Firms that handed the project to whoever had spare time reported abandonment rates near half. Those that named a single owner with authority to change how work is done reported under fifteen percent.

questions.question: What is the main point of the article?
options: Spreadsheets are being prohibited by regulators
Large systems now cost less than small ones
Small manufacturers are replacing manual methods for practical reasons
Most small firms have already finished modernizing
questions.explanation: The article explains why small manufacturers are leaving spreadsheets behind, naming customer demands, insurer requirements, and retirements. No regulator is mentioned, so the first option invents a cause.

questions.question: According to the article, what do insurers ask small manufacturers to provide?
options: Traceability records
Electronic order confirmations
Annual spending reports
The name of a project owner
questions.explanation: The second paragraph assigns traceability records to insurers and electronic order confirmations to large customers. Mixing those two up produces the second option, which is the most tempting wrong answer.

questions.question: What does the article suggest about projects that succeed?
options: They cost more than 100,000 dollars in the first year
They cover every department at the same time
They are led by consultants hired from outside
They have one person clearly in charge
questions.explanation: Abandonment falls below fifteen percent when a single owner with real authority runs the project. The median first-year spend of 31,000 dollars contradicts the option about six-figure budgets.
